passage: Disha handed Mehak the village-survey questionnaire on the bus to the college in the kasba, and her stomach fluttered. It was the part she had planned for weeks. "Let's look at your first ten forms on Wednesday," Disha said, "and again on Friday." Mehak nodded. Twice that week Disha's fingers hovered over her phone to ask if it was done. She put it down. On Wednesday the forms had gaps in three answers. "These are good. Could we make the age question clearer?" Mehak laughed. "I noticed that too." By Friday the sheet was tidy.

qa.q: When did Disha and Mehak agree to look at the first ten forms?
qa.a: They agreed to look at them on Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling as she handed over the questionnaire?
qa.a: Her stomach fluttered, showing nervous hope, since it was the part she had planned for weeks.

qa.q: How did the checkpoints help the group?
qa.a: They gave fixed times to review the work, so Disha did not have to keep asking and Mehak could fix the gaps early.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel about how Disha gave feedback?
qa.a: Mehak probably felt trusted, since Disha praised the forms first and asked kindly about the age question.

grounding: A groupmate hands over a part and hopes it is done well, agreeing checkpoints and giving kind feedback without micromanaging.

passage:
When our team split the documentary project, I handed the editing to Gopika. Then I watched every second. I messaged her four times a day: "Did you trim the intro?" "Use the other music." "Can you send me the file?" On Wednesday she replied, "Do you want to just do it yourself?" and went offline.
That stung, because she was right. I didn't trust anyone with my idea.
I called her that night and apologised. We agreed on two checkpoints instead: a rough cut on Friday and a final cut on Monday, and I would comment only then. When the rough cut came, I wrote three notes, starting with what I loved, the way she opened on the fisherwoman's hands. Then two changes.
The final version was better than mine would have been. I told her so.
— Vasudha

qa.q: How many times a day did Vasudha message Gopika?
Why did Gopika's reply sting Vasudha?
qa.a: Because it was true: Vasudha felt exposed and embarrassed at not trusting anyone with the idea.

qa.q: What did Vasudha and Gopika agree on?
qa.a: Two checkpoints, a rough cut on Friday and a final on Monday, with comments only then, starting with what worked.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel about the constant messages?
qa.a: Frustrated and mistrusted, enough to ask "Do you want to just do it yourself?" and go offline.

grounding: Shows handing over part of a project, the pitfall of micromanaging, and agreeing checkpoints and giving kind feedback instead.

passage:
Lab supervisor's note, robotics club, 3 March
This week I watched Manoj, the team captain, hand the motor-control code to Hrithik, a second-year. Last year Manoj rewrote other people's code at midnight without telling them, and the team nearly fell apart.
This time was different. On Monday Manoj said, "It's yours. Can we check on Wednesday and Friday? I'll only look then." On Wednesday Hrithik's code made the robot spin in circles. Manoj laughed, then said, "Your structure is clean. The turning speed is too high. Want to try halving it?" He didn't touch the keyboard.
On Friday the robot ran the course in forty seconds. Hrithik looked proud; Manoj looked like someone trying hard not to interfere, and mostly succeeding.
I told Manoj afterwards that this is what leadership looks like. I have asked him to share the checkpoint idea at next week's club meeting.

qa.q: How long did the robot take to run the course on Friday?
What did Manoj seem to feel on Friday?
qa.a: Proud of Hrithik and a little restless, trying hard not to interfere.

qa.q: How did Manoj give feedback kindly on Wednesday?
qa.a: He laughed, praised the clean structure first, named one problem, the turning speed, and suggested a fix without touching the keyboard.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel about being trusted with the code?
qa.a: Proud and capable, especially when the robot finished the course.

grounding: Illustrates trusting a teammate with a part, agreeing on checkpoints and giving kind feedback instead of micromanaging.
